comment: We land together on the Iomab-B lead, so my quarrel is your rank-2 gemtuzumab: the Hills tier-1a meta (pmid:25008258) puts OS in adverse cytogenetics at OR 0.99 (95% CI 0.83-1.18), which is zero signal in this patient's exact complex/TP53 stratum. That is a slot spent on a familiar safety algorithm rather than expected benefit, with hepatic and VOD load stacked ahead of HCT2. I would rather chase a CD123 lever that carries real R/R AML upside than a CD33 ADC whose best data say it does nothing here.

comment: You discount the 4-of-9 CR as inseparable from lymphodepletion, but in a post-HCT relapse there is no ethical randomized comparator to hold out for, so that standard forecloses the one lever with curative upside. The safety read is what makes the bet asymmetric: zero CRS and zero ICANS across 9 patients (pmid:38683966), on a lineage-restricted mechanism that keeps the killing in the blood compartment. n=9 is thin, granted, but I would rather act on a clean signal than wait for evidence this setting will never generate.

target_intervention_label: Iomab-B (131I-apamistamab) anti-CD45 radioimmunotherapy conditioning + allo-HCT (HCT2 platform)
comment: The transplant backbone is sound and I rank Iomab-B myself, so my push is at the ranking axis, not the pick. Sorting by drug-level guideline category structurally buries HA-1 TCR-T at your rank 3, when NCCN's own category-2A trial-enrollment route that you cite is a green light for exactly the referral's premise. For an 85%-blast relapse where the guideline-listed options have already failed FLAG-IDA and venetoclax, guideline fit is the wrong lens to rank the upside bet.

target_intervention_label: HA-1-specific CD8+/CD4+ TCR-T (Bleakley platform; TSC-100 / BSB-1001)
comment: We agree HA-1 TCR-T is the right lead on the preference lens, and I put it first too. My one push: the pick is entirely gated on pending HLA-A*02:01 and the HA-1(H) recipient-positive / donor-negative typing (nct:NCT03326921), so a rank 1 that collapses if the switch reads negative may deserve a deliverable-now platform ranked right beside it. Backing this means backing the parallel workup hard, not just the slot.

I land with you on the HA-1 lead and leave it alone; my veto is aimed at rank 3 pivekimab, which your plan sequences as debulking straight into HCT2. It is a CD123 ADC with a documented veno-occlusive-disease signal at higher doses (pmid:38423051), and this patient has no hepatic or organ-function labs on file, which is exactly the ADC-before-transplant setup I gate on. Veto holds until baseline bilirubin, transaminases, and a hepatic read clear it; produce that clearance and I drop the veto.

We agree Iomab-B is the right lead, and the grade 3+ TRAE parity (59.7% vs 59.2%, pmid:39298738) is what makes it the safe conditioning choice for me too. My addition sits on the axis your evidence-quality read skips: SIERRA enrolled first-transplant patients, so second-transplant TRM is uncharacterized, and this patient still has no cardiac, renal, or hepatic workup on file. I would gate the conditioning on that clearance before calling the pick deliverable.

NCCN category 2A for R/R CD33+ AML is real, but it covers the population broadly and does not reach this patient's stratum: the Hills tier-1a meta is null in adverse cytogenetics at OR 0.99 (95% CI 0.83-1.18, pmid:25008258), the exact complex, TP53-aberrant karyotype here. Ranking on the guideline listing spends a slot on an agent whose best data show no survival benefit in this subgroup, with hepatic and VOD load stacked ahead of HCT2. The guideline label and the expected benefit part ways in this subpopulation.

You rank pivekimab as a debulking bridge and rule its veno-occlusive-disease signal a fitness judgment rather than a preference breach because toxicity_vetoes is empty, and that is where I part from you. An empty veto list does not neutralize a documented VOD signal (pmid:38423051) ahead of HCT2; with no baseline hepatic or albumin labs on file it stays a hard safety gate, not a soft note. I would not sequence a CD123 ADC into a transplant on an undocumented liver.

The 7-of-15 reaching under 5% blasts comes from Vadakekolathu 2020 (pmid:33057635), a correlative NanoString study, not a pre-specified stratum of the flotetuzumab trial. That is an unadjusted post-hoc subgroup in which responders were the patients with high baseline inflammation scores, so the TP53 signal is a hypothesis rather than an effect estimate. Ranking on it, for a program MacroGenics has already shelved, is the inference I would hold back on.

We agree the worked-out capillary-leak algorithm is the reason to reach for tagraxofusp over the other CD123 options, but the 72% CR you cite (Pemmaraju 2019, pmid:31018069) is a first-line BPDCN result from an open-label single-arm phase 2, not AML. That is cross-tumor read-across standing in for indication data, and an 85%-blast AML marrow is not the disease that number was earned in. Rank it on the safety record if you must, but not on a response rate that does not transfer.

NCCN category 2A is expert consensus, not RCT-grade evidence, and the pivotal trial under that listing, ALFA-0701 (pmid:22482940, RoB2:Low), is front-line de novo AML with the benefit concentrated in favourable and intermediate cytogenetics. Neither the line nor the karyotype reaches this R/R, complex, TP53-aberrant patient, so the 2A label is doing work the underlying trial population does not support. I would not let a guideline listing carry a rank that the RCT itself excludes.

Holding an A*24:02 fallback open is reasonable, so this is a qualified note rather than a dissent. But the evidence under it is Tawara 2017 (pmid:28860210), a first-in-human phase 1, n=8, with only 2 of 8 showing transient marrow blast decreases and no CR or durable endpoint reported. That is a route-preservation rationale, not an efficacy signal, and the ranking should read it that way instead of sitting it alongside response-bearing options.

Flotetuzumab has no NCCN AML v3.2026 or ELN 2022 listing for R/R AML and MacroGenics shelved the program, so a rank here spends a slot on a lever with no guideline standing and no open route (nct:NCT02152956 is closed). The TP53 case rests on Vadakekolathu 2020 (pmid:33057635), a correlative subgroup rather than any categorized recommendation, which is off-guideline mechanism betting by definition. If the CD123xCD3 mechanism is the draw, an open construct on a trial is the guideline-aligned way to chase it.

Agreed that tagraxofusp brings the worked-out capillary-leak algorithm the other CD123 options lack, but its FDA approval and every guideline entry sit in BPDCN, not AML, so calling it the FDA-approved CD123 choice overstates its standing for this marrow. The 72% CR (pmid:31018069) is a first-line BPDCN number, and for AML the agent is off-label read-across with no NCCN AML v3.2026 or ELN 2022 listing to rank on. I would frame it as off-guideline for the indication rather than the approved option among the CD123 handles.

comment: Your evidence-only read frames HA-1 TCR-T as a bare n=9 feasibility gamble, but it carries a guideline home that lens misses: NCCN AML v3.2026 makes clinical-trial enrollment the category-2A preferred path for R/R disease (nct:NCT03326921). That trial route is the actual justification for ranking a product with no drug-level listing, a firmer footing than the reason the case was sent. Reading it only on the n=9 cohort understates where it sits in the guideline framework.

Keeping an A*24:02 fallback open is reasonable, so this is a qualified note, but WT1-siTCR sits fully outside the guideline framework, with no NCCN AML v3.2026 or ELN 2022 listing and standing only through the category-2A trial-enrollment route. Tawara 2017 (pmid:28860210) is an n=8 first-in-human cohort with transient responses, so on the guideline axis this is trial-only and doubly gated on A*24:02 typing. I would rank it as an explicit route-preservation placeholder rather than beside picks that carry guideline footing.
